title: Midterm waves are the rule, not the exception
contentHtml:
In the history of Silver Bulletin/FiveThirtyEight election forecasts, I’m not sure there’s ever really been a case where we’ve been completely on the other side of the conventional wisdom — in other words, when our model favored Republicans, but everyone else thought Democrats were going to win, or vice versa.

Instead, since models like FLIPR are probabilistic, the difference tends to be in the degree of confidence or conviction. We’ve been on either side of that equation. In 2016, as much as these pleas sometimes fell on deaf ears, we spent a lot of time emphasizing that Hillary Clinton’s lead was much less secure than most people assumed, and our model gave Donald Trump considerably better chances than prediction markets and other quantitative forecasts. In 2020, the opposite was true. Everyone was bracing for a 2016-like polling error, but Joe Biden’s lead in the polls was so large that he could withstand a 2016-magnitude polling error and still prevail. And that’s basically what happened: general election polls were actually more biased in 2020 than in 2016, but Biden’s lead was big enough to absorb the blow.

In other cycles, we’ve been pretty much aligned with the zeitgeist. For instance, there weren’t many differences of opinion between the FiveThirtyEight model and the CW in Trump’s previous midterm in 2018. While it’s slightly less “fun,” it’s nice when this happens. I’m not sure I need the stress of another round of Model Wars.

The 2026 election initially looked like one of those less contentious cases. When we launched FLIPR on Aug. 11, Democrats had about a 55 percent chance of winning the Senate and 85 percent in the House. Both numbers were within a few percentage points of what prediction markets said at the time1. It was an easy story to tell — the House was probably going to flip, but that was hardly a bold prediction considering the history of the midterms, as I’ll discuss later in today’s column. And the Senate? Well, it was a toss-up.

But after several weeks of extremely strong polling for Democrats, FLIPR is now “picking a side” and telling a much more confident story.

Pretty much every day since Labor Day (Sept. 7), Democrats’ lead on the generic ballot has expanded. On Sept. 7, they led by 6.5 points; now that lead has expanded to 8.9 points. It’s not particularly hard to explain this: look at what’s happening with Trump’s approval rating or with gas and diesel prices. Still, that’s approximately a two-and-a-half point shift, which is already bigger than the post-Labor Day swing in most recent midterms.2

And some polls have Democrats’ lead climbing into the double-digits or even the mid-teens: D +12, D +13, D +14 and even D +15 are some numbers we’ve seen printed recently, and they mostly come from highly-rated pollsters. Democrats’ numbers also tend to be stronger in surveys of likely voters, something that FLIPR adjusts for but our standard generic ballot average does not. With the likely-voter adjustment turned on, Democrats’ lead grows to 9.6 points.

FLIPR does hedge against this slightly: the generic ballot is the single most important input to FLIPR, but not its “final answer”; it’s blended with lots of other data. So our forecast of the House popular vote isn’t quite as rosy for Democrats: D +7.9. (There’s a wonky section explaining the difference at the end of today’s story.) Still, the trend in our forecast has been unmistakable, particularly in the Senate:3
